newsitem.title: USA: Calif. panel okays utility deregulation proposal.
newsitem.headline: Calif. panel okays utility deregulation proposal.

text.p: A key panel of California lawmakers approved legislation on Tuesday that would help investor-owned utilities write-off "stranded" costs to better compete in a deregulated California market.
The joint Senate-Assembly conference committee voted 6-to-0 in favour of the legislation that would deregulate California's massive electric power industry while cutting consumer rates by 10 percent.
The landmark legislation was expected to be voted on in the full Senate and Assembly later this week.

The legislation, if approved by the full Senate and Assembly and signed by Governor Pete Wilson, would provide the foundation for transforming the regulatory framework of the state's electric industry, creating a new market structure and ending the utility monopoly on generation.
Senate President Pro Tem Bill Lockyer, D-Hayward, pronounced the electric industry restructuring legislation "the most significant economic measure of the year."
"This is designed to reduce costs to all consumers of all classes and simultaneously bring stability to the system," said Senator Steve Peace, conference committee chairman.
A Wilson spokesman indicated on Tuesday that the Republican governor was supportive of the legislation.
Under the legislation, electric utility customers in the state would have a choice of providers. Under the proposal, however, municipal utilities would not be required to open their markets.
To help investor-owned utilities in the state write-off their stranded costs, a statewide competitive transition charge would be enacted, said David Takashima, chief of staff for Senator Peace.
While in place, investor-owned utility rates would be frozen. The funds would be used by the utilities to write-off stranded costs such as nuclear power plants and certain power purchase contracts.

Initially, the utilities could issue through the state infrastructure bank an estimated $5 billion in revenue bonds backed by the transition charge, according to Takashima. He said the utilities could issue additional "rate reduction bonds" later, for a total of up to $10 billion.
The proposed financings would provide savings to the utilities, and those savings, under the legislation, would be passed on to customers, Takashima said.
The legislation provides for rate savings for residential and small commercial consumers by mandating a no less than 10 percent rate reduction lasting for five years.
According to the legislation, residential and small commercial ratepayers would receive a total cumulative rate reduction of no less than 20 percent by April 1, 2002.
"We had 20 days of hearings and over 100 hours of discussion on a bill that is a compromise for everyone. But I think everyone benefits," Takashima said.
